## Presentation setup {.hidden data-visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: presentation-data-setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(ggrepel)
  library(gt)
  library(htmlwidgets)
  library(plotly)
  library(scales)
  library(stringr)
  library(tidyr)
})

# Shared visual tokens and chart styling

category_colours <- c(
  "Everyday materials" = "#005EB8",
  "Industrial/construction" = "#C45113",
  "Organic/landscape" = "#00875A",
  "Process/other" = "#8F3D7A"
)

effect_colours <- c(
  "Mix effect (composition changed)" = "#D55E00",
  "Performance effect (stream rates changed)" = "#0072B2"
)

system_colours <- c(
  "recycling" = "#0F766E",
  "disposal_action" = "#B4531F",
  "neutral" = "#8D9A98"
)

source_note <-
  "Source: MSE and NEA, Waste Management And Overall Recycling Rates, Annual, via SingStat/Data.gov.sg."

slide_chart_theme <- theme_minimal(base_family = "sans", base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#d7e3df", linewidth = 0.4),
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      colour = "#17212b",
      size = 18
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#607173", size = 13),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#17212b", size = 13.5),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#263238", size = 12.5),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11.5),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#607173", size = 10),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)
  )

stream_categories <- tibble(
  waste_stream = c(
    "Construction & Demolition", "Ferrous Metal", "Non-Ferrous Metal",
    "Used Slag", "Scrap Tyres", "Horticultural", "Wood",
    "Paper/Cardboard", "Glass", "Food", "Textile/Leather", "Plastic",
    "Ash And Sludge", "Others"
  ),
  waste_system_category = c(
    rep("Industrial/construction", 5),
    rep("Organic/landscape", 2),
    rep("Everyday materials", 5),
    rep("Process/other", 2)
  )
)

# Source ingestion and tidy stream-year model

# pipeline-step-1-start
raw_waste <- read.csv(
  "data/waste_management.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("na", "NA", "")
)
# pipeline-step-1-end

# pipeline-step-2-start
block_names <- c(
  "Total Generated", "Total Recycled", "Total Disposed", "Recycling Rate"
)

raw_tagged <- raw_waste |>
  mutate(metric = if_else(
    DataSeries %in% block_names,
    DataSeries,
    NA_character_
  )) |>
  fill(metric)
# pipeline-step-2-end

national_year <- raw_tagged |>
  filter(DataSeries %in% block_names) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  select(metric = DataSeries, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  rename(
    generated = `Total Generated`,
    recycled = `Total Recycled`,
    disposed = `Total Disposed`,
    source_recycling_rate = `Recycling Rate`
  )

decade_rate_data <- national_year |>
  filter(year %in% 2014:2024) |>
  arrange(year)

rate_event_annotations <- tibble(
  year = c(2020, 2022, 2023, 2024),
  source_recycling_rate = c(52, 57, 52, 50),
  label_x = c(2019.55, 2021.65, 2022.95, 2024.55),
  label_y = c(59.5, 68.0, 62.5, 57.0),
  label_anchor_y = c(56.6, 65.5, 59.5, 54.0),
  point_anchor_x = c(2019.96, 2021.98, 2023.00, 2024.06),
  point_anchor_y = c(52.45, 57.45, 52.45, 50.45),
  label = c(
    "Circuit Breaker paused\nconstruction and industrial\nactivity [1]",
    "Construction and demolition\nactivity picked up again [2]",
    "Fewer demolition projects cut\nconstruction waste by more\nthan 40% [3]",
    "Less demolition and steel\nsmelting reduced highly\nrecycled waste [4]"
  )
)

decade_rate_plot <- ggplot(
  decade_rate_data,
  aes(x = year, y = source_recycling_rate)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = 48, ymax = source_recycling_rate),
    fill = "#e3f0ec"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    colour = unname(system_colours["recycling"]),
    linewidth = 1.15
  ) +
  geom_point(
    colour = unname(system_colours["recycling"]),
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = decade_rate_data |> filter(year == 2024),
    colour = unname(system_colours["disposal_action"]),
    size = 3.8
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = rate_event_annotations,
    aes(
      x = label_x,
      xend = point_anchor_x,
      y = label_anchor_y,
      yend = point_anchor_y
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    arrow = grid::arrow(
      angle = 25,
      length = grid::unit(0.09, "inches"),
      type = "closed"
    ),
    colour = "#263238",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = rate_event_annotations,
    aes(x = label_x, y = label_y, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "#111111",
    fill = "#ffffff",
    fontface = "plain",
    label.padding = grid::unit(0.14, "lines"),
    label.r = grid::unit(0, "lines"),
    label.size = 0.35,
    lineheight = 0.96,
    size = 4.6
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(2014, 2024, 2),
    labels = seq(2014, 2024, 2),
    limits = c(2013.6, 2025.75),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(50, 55, 60, 65, 70),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(46, 72), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "sans", base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#465556", size = 10.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      colour = "#dce5e2",
      linewidth = 0.45
    ),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(4, 8, 3, 5)
  )

# pipeline-step-3-start
stream_year <- raw_tagged |>
  filter(!DataSeries %in% block_names) |>
  mutate(waste_stream = str_trim(DataSeries)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  select(waste_stream, year, metric, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  rename(
    generated = `Total Generated`,
    recycled = `Total Recycled`,
    disposed = `Total Disposed`,
    source_recycling_rate = `Recycling Rate`
  ) |>
  left_join(stream_categories, by = "waste_stream") |>
  mutate(
    exact_recycling_rate = recycled / generated,
    generated_kt = generated / 1000,
    recycled_kt = recycled / 1000,
    disposed_kt = disposed / 1000
  )
# pipeline-step-3-end

# pipeline-step-4-start
national_reference <- national_year |>
  transmute(
    year,
    national_recycling_rate = source_recycling_rate,
    national_recycled = recycled,
    national_disposed = disposed
  )

# Priority-map fields and 2024 evidence cards

priority_stream_year <- stream_year |>
  filter(year %in% 2014:2024, !is.na(source_recycling_rate)) |>
  left_join(national_reference, by = "year") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    median_generated_kt = median(generated_kt),
    recycling_rate = source_recycling_rate,
    recycling_share = recycled / national_recycled,
    disposal_share = disposed / national_disposed,
    rate_gap = recycling_rate - national_recycling_rate,
    priority_group = case_when(
      generated_kt > median_generated_kt &
        recycling_rate < national_recycling_rate ~
          "High-volume, low-recycling",
      recycling_rate < national_recycling_rate ~ "Disposal concern",
      TRUE ~ "Higher recycling"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()
# pipeline-step-4-end

priority_stream_year <- priority_stream_year |>
  mutate(
    Year = factor(year, levels = 2014:2024),
    waste_system_category = factor(
      waste_system_category,
      levels = names(category_colours)
    ),
    jitter_id = match(
      waste_stream,
      sort(unique(priority_stream_year$waste_stream))
    ),
    generated_plot_kt = pmax(
      0,
      generated_kt + (((jitter_id * 37) %% 11) - 5) * 2
    ),
    recycling_rate_plot = pmin(
      100,
      pmax(
        0,
        recycling_rate + (((jitter_id * 53) %% 9) - 4) * 0.35
      )
    ),
    chart_label = case_when(
      waste_stream == "Construction & Demolition" ~
        "Construction & Demolition",
      waste_stream == "Ash And Sludge" ~ "Ash & Sludge",
      waste_stream == "Non-Ferrous Metal" ~ "Non-ferrous metal",
      TRUE ~ waste_stream
    ),
    label_colour = unname(
      category_colours[as.character(waste_system_category)]
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", waste_stream, "</b><br>",
      "Waste Stream Category: ", waste_system_category, "<br>",
      "Generated: ", format(round(generated_kt), big.mark = ","), " kt<br>",
      "Recycled: ", format(round(recycled_kt), big.mark = ","), " kt<br>",
      "Disposed: ", format(round(disposed_kt), big.mark = ","), " kt<br>",
      "Recycling rate: ", recycling_rate, "%<br>",
      "Gap from national rate: ",
      if_else(rate_gap > 0, "+", ""),
      format(round(rate_gap, 1), nsmall = 1), " pp<br>",
      "Share of national disposal: ",
      scales::percent(disposal_share, accuracy = 0.1), "<br>",
      "Share of national recycling: ",
      scales::percent(recycling_share, accuracy = 0.1), "<br>",
      "Screening group: ", priority_group
    )
  )

priority_2024 <- priority_stream_year |>
  filter(year == 2024)

priority_card_copy <- tibble(
  waste_stream = c("Plastic", "Paper/Cardboard", "Food"),
  display_order = 1:3,
  card_class = c("priority-plastic", "priority-paper", "priority-food"),
  why_text = c(
    "Lowest recovery, so almost all generated volume remains.",
    "Greater volume leaves almost the same disposal as plastic.",
    "Smaller scale, but weak recovery still leaves substantial disposed tonnage."
  )
)

priority_card_data <- priority_2024 |>
  inner_join(priority_card_copy, by = "waste_stream") |>
  arrange(display_order)

top_disposal_2024 <- stream_year |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  arrange(desc(disposed_kt)) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(waste_stream)

screened_streams_2024 <- priority_2024 |>
  filter(priority_group == "High-volume, low-recycling") |>
  arrange(desc(disposed_kt)) |>
  pull(waste_stream)

priority_card_scale_kt <- ceiling(
  max(priority_card_data$generated_kt) / 100
) * 100

priority_card_data <- priority_card_data |>
  mutate(
    rank = sprintf("%02d", display_order),
    disposed_rate = 100 - recycling_rate,
    generated_width = generated_kt / priority_card_scale_kt * 100,
    disposed_width = disposed_kt / priority_card_scale_kt * 100
  )

priority_card_summary <- priority_card_data |>
  summarise(
    disposed_kt = sum(disposed_kt),
    disposal_share = sum(disposal_share)
  )

priority_cards_html <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(priority_card_data)),
  function(i) {
    card <- priority_card_data[i, ]
    rate_label <- number(card$recycling_rate, accuracy = 1)
    disposed_rate_label <- number(card$disposed_rate, accuracy = 1)
    generated_label <- format(
      round(card$generated_kt),
      big.mark = ",",
      scientific = FALSE,
      trim = TRUE
    )
    disposed_label <- format(
      round(card$disposed_kt),
      big.mark = ",",
      scientific = FALSE,
      trim = TRUE
    )
    scale_label <- format(
      priority_card_scale_kt,
      big.mark = ",",
      scientific = FALSE,
      trim = TRUE
    )
    generated_width_label <- number(card$generated_width, accuracy = 0.1)
    disposed_width_label <- number(card$disposed_width, accuracy = 0.1)
    disposal_share_label <- percent(card$disposal_share, accuracy = 0.1)

    paste0(
      '<div class="priority-stream ', card$card_class, '">',
      '<span class="priority-rank">', card$rank, '</span>',
      '<h3>', card$waste_stream, '</h3>',
      '<div class="priority-rate-row">',
      '<span class="priority-rate">', rate_label, '%</span>',
      '<span class="priority-rate-label">recycling rate</span>',
      '</div>',
      '<div class="priority-composition" aria-label="',
      rate_label, ' percent recycled and approximately ',
      disposed_rate_label, ' percent disposed">',
      '<i class="priority-recycled" style="width:', rate_label, '%"></i>',
      '<i class="priority-disposed" style="width:',
      disposed_rate_label, '%"></i>',
      '</div>',
      '<div class="priority-composition-labels">',
      '<span>', rate_label, '% recycled</span>',
      '<span>≈', disposed_rate_label, '% disposed</span>',
      '</div>',
      '<div class="priority-volume-comparison" aria-label="',
      'Generated and disposed tonnage on a common zero to ',
      scale_label, ' kilotonne scale">',
      '<span class="priority-scale-label">Common scale: 0–',
      scale_label, ' kt</span>',
      '<div class="priority-volume-row">',
      '<span>Generated</span><b><i style="width:',
      generated_width_label, '%"></i></b><strong>',
      generated_label, ' kt</strong>',
      '</div>',
      '<div class="priority-volume-row priority-volume-disposed">',
      '<span>Disposed</span><b><i style="width:',
      disposed_width_label, '%"></i></b><strong>',
      disposed_label, ' kt</strong>',
      '</div>',
      '<div class="priority-share-note"><strong>',
      disposal_share_label,
      '</strong> of national disposal</div>',
      '</div>',
      '<p><strong>Why it matters:</strong> ', card$why_text, '</p>',
      '</div>'
    )
  },
  character(1)
)

priority_cards_html <- paste(priority_cards_html, collapse = "\n")

priority_summary_html <- paste0(
  '<div class="priority-total">',
  '<span><strong>',
  percent(priority_card_summary$disposal_share, accuracy = 0.1),
  '</strong><small>of national disposal</small></span>',
  '<span><strong>',
  number(priority_card_summary$disposed_kt / 1000, accuracy = 0.01),
  ' million tonnes</strong>',
  '<small>still requiring incineration or landfill</small></span>',
  '<p>They are the only streams in the high-volume, low-recycling area and ',
  'also the three largest contributors to national disposal.</p>',
  '</div>'
)

# Recycling-versus-disposal contribution comparison

contribution_mismatch <- stream_year |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  left_join(
    national_reference |> filter(year == 2024),
    by = "year"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    recycling_share = recycled / national_recycled,
    disposal_share = disposed / national_disposed,
    contribution_gap = disposal_share - recycling_share,
    label_flag = waste_stream %in% c(
      "Plastic",
      "Paper/Cardboard",
      "Food",
      "Ferrous Metal",
      "Construction & Demolition",
      "Used Slag",
      "Wood"
    )
  )

contribution_gap_limit <- max(
  abs(contribution_mismatch$contribution_gap),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

disposal_recycling_plot <- ggplot(
  contribution_mismatch,
  aes(x = disposal_share, y = recycling_share)
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    colour = "#607173",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.65
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.275,
    y = 0.205,
    label = "More disposal contribution",
    colour = unname(system_colours["disposal_action"]),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.135,
    y = 0.135,
    label = "Equal contribution to recycling and disposal",
    angle = 24,
    colour = "#263238",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.35,
    vjust = -0.60
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.065,
    y = 0.395,
    label = "More recycling contribution",
    colour = unname(system_colours["recycling"]),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.305,
    y = 0.078,
    label = "Plastic + paper/cardboard + food\n71.8% of national disposal",
    colour = unname(system_colours["disposal_action"]),
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 1,
    lineheight = 1.05,
    size = 3.45
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(fill = contribution_gap, size = generated_kt),
    shape = 21,
    colour = "#263238",
    stroke = 0.45,
    alpha = 0.96,
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.0012,
      height = 0.0012,
      seed = 2024
    ),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = if_else(label_flag, waste_stream, "")),
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.0012,
      height = 0.0012,
      seed = 2024
    ),
    seed = 2024,
    box.padding = 0.28,
    point.padding = 0.18,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    force = 0.8,
    force_pull = 0.5,
    segment.colour = "#879694",
    segment.linewidth = 0.32,
    size = 3.7,
    colour = "#263238",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = unname(system_colours["recycling"]),
    mid = unname(system_colours["neutral"]),
    high = unname(system_colours["disposal_action"]),
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-contribution_gap_limit, contribution_gap_limit),
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    name = "Contribution gap\n(disposal − recycling)"
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 11, breaks = c(300, 800, 1200)) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_colourbar(
      title.position = "top",
      barheight = grid::unit(42, "mm"),
      barwidth = grid::unit(4.5, "mm"),
      order = 1
    ),
    size = guide_legend(
      title.position = "top",
      order = 2,
      override.aes = list(
        fill = "#263238",
        colour = "#263238",
        alpha = 1
      )
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 0.30, 0.10),
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 0.40, 0.10),
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(-0.012, 0.33),
    ylim = c(-0.015, 0.43),
    expand = FALSE,
    clip = "on"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    x = "Share of national disposed waste",
    y = "Share of national recycled waste",
    size = "Generated waste\n('000 tonnes)",
    caption = NULL
  ) +
  slide_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.15, "lines"),
    legend.key.height = grid::unit(0.75, "lines"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5),
    plot.margin = margin(4, 8, 8, 10)
  )

plot_to_inline_svg <- function(plot, width, height) {
  svg_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".svg")

  grDevices::svg(
    filename = svg_path,
    width = width,
    height = height,
    onefile = TRUE,
    bg = "transparent"
  )
  print(plot)
  grDevices::dev.off()

  svg_lines <- readLines(svg_path, warn = FALSE)
  unlink(svg_path)

  svg_start <- grep("^<svg", svg_lines)[1]
  stopifnot(!is.na(svg_start))

  paste(svg_lines[svg_start:length(svg_lines)], collapse = "\n")
}

disposal_recycling_svg <- plot_to_inline_svg(
  disposal_recycling_plot,
  width = 11.5,
  height = 5.8
)

# Persistent rate-gap heatmap

p2_stream_order <- c(
  "Non-Ferrous Metal",
  "Ferrous Metal",
  "Construction & Demolition",
  "Used Slag",
  "Scrap Tyres",
  "Horticultural",
  "Wood",
  "Paper/Cardboard",
  "Food",
  "Ash And Sludge",
  "Glass",
  "Plastic",
  "Textile/Leather"
)

p2_rate_gap <- priority_stream_year |>
  filter(
    year >= 2014,
    year <= 2024,
    waste_stream %in% p2_stream_order
  ) |>
  mutate(
    waste_stream = factor(
      waste_stream,
      levels = rev(p2_stream_order)
    ),
    displayed_gap = if_else(rate_gap < -55, NA_real_, rate_gap),
    gap_label = paste0(
      if_else(rate_gap > 0, "+", ""),
      round(rate_gap)
    )
  )

p2_spearman_rho <- cor(
  priority_2024$generated_kt,
  priority_2024$recycling_rate,
  method = "spearman"
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(p2_rate_gap) == 143,
  round(p2_spearman_rho, 3) == 0.017
)

p2_colour_for_gap <- function(gap) {
  if (gap < -55) {
    return("#858585")
  }

  if (gap <= 0) {
    colour_value <- grDevices::colorRamp(
      c("#e66a00", "#f7f4f1"),
      space = "Lab"
    )((gap + 55) / 55)
  } else {
    colour_value <- grDevices::colorRamp(
      c("#f7f4f1", "#2f78b7"),
      space = "Lab"
    )(gap / 50)
  }

  grDevices::rgb(
    colour_value[1] / 255,
    colour_value[2] / 255,
    colour_value[3] / 255
  )
}

p2_rate_gap_native <- p2_rate_gap |>
  mutate(

# Counterfactual and symmetric shift-share analysis

endpoints <- stream_year |>
  filter(year %in% c(2014, 2024)) |>
  select(waste_stream, year, generated, exact_recycling_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(generated, exact_recycling_rate),
    names_glue = "{.value}_{year}"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    weight_2014 = generated_2014 / sum(generated_2014),
    weight_2024 = generated_2024 / sum(generated_2024)
  )

counterfactual_rate <- endpoints |>
  summarise(
    value = sum(weight_2014 * exact_recycling_rate_2024)
  ) |>
  pull(value)

reconstructed_rate_2014 <- sum(
  endpoints$weight_2014 * endpoints$exact_recycling_rate_2014
)
reconstructed_rate_2024 <- sum(
  endpoints$weight_2024 * endpoints$exact_recycling_rate_2024
)

rate_effect_counterfactual <-
  counterfactual_rate - reconstructed_rate_2014
mix_effect_counterfactual <-
  reconstructed_rate_2024 - counterfactual_rate

counterfactual_plot_data <- tibble(
  scenario = factor(
    c(
      "2014 reconstructed",
      "2024 counterfactual\n(2014 mix, 2024 rates)",
      "2024 reconstructed"
    ),
    levels = c(
      "2014 reconstructed",
      "2024 counterfactual\n(2014 mix, 2024 rates)",
      "2024 reconstructed"
    )
  ),
  rate = c(
    reconstructed_rate_2014,
    counterfactual_rate,
    reconstructed_rate_2024
  ),
  fill = c("Actual", "Counterfactual", "Actual")
)

counterfactual_chart <- ggplot(
  counterfactual_plot_data,
  aes(x = scenario, y = rate)
) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = fill), width = 0.58) +
  geom_line(
    aes(group = 1),
    colour = "#607173",
    linewidth = 0.65,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.35,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 5,
    colour = "#17212b"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.5,
    y = 0.625,
    label = paste0(
      "Rates changed: ",
      number(rate_effect_counterfactual * 100, accuracy = 0.1),
      " pp"
    ),
    colour = unname(
      effect_colours["Performance effect (stream rates changed)"]
    ),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4.3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.5,
    y = 0.575,
    label = paste0(
      "Then mix changed: ",
      number(mix_effect_counterfactual * 100, accuracy = 0.1),
      " pp"
    ),
    colour = unname(
      effect_colours["Mix effect (composition changed)"]
    ),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Actual" = "#17212b", "Counterfactual" = "#9aa6a4"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6),
    limits = c(0, 0.68),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Holding the waste mix at 2014 levels keeps 2024 near 57%",
    subtitle = "A sequential counterfactual check using rates calculated from published tonnage",
    x = NULL,
    y = "National recycling rate",
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  slide_chart_theme +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#e4e7e6"),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 8, 10)
  )

shift_share <- endpoints |>
  mutate(
    mix_effect_pp =
      (weight_2024 - weight_2014) *
      (exact_recycling_rate_2014 + exact_recycling_rate_2024) / 2 * 100,
    rate_effect_pp =
      (exact_recycling_rate_2024 - exact_recycling_rate_2014) *
      (weight_2014 + weight_2024) / 2 * 100,
    total_contribution_pp = mix_effect_pp + rate_effect_pp
  ) |>
  arrange(total_contribution_pp)

shift_share_total <- shift_share |>
  summarise(
    mix_effect_pp = sum(mix_effect_pp),
    rate_effect_pp = sum(rate_effect_pp),
    total_contribution_pp = sum(total_contribution_pp)
  )

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    shift_share_total$total_contribution_pp,
    (reconstructed_rate_2024 - reconstructed_rate_2014) * 100,
    tolerance = 1e-8
  ))
)

shift_share_long <- shift_share |>
  mutate(
    waste_stream = factor(waste_stream, levels = waste_stream)
  ) |>
  select(
    waste_stream,
    total_contribution_pp,
    `Mix effect (composition changed)` = mix_effect_pp,
    `Performance effect (stream rates changed)` = rate_effect_pp
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      `Mix effect (composition changed)`,
      `Performance effect (stream rates changed)`
    ),
    names_to = "effect",
    values_to = "contribution_pp"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    effect = factor(
      effect,
      levels = c(
        "Mix effect (composition changed)",
        "Performance effect (stream rates changed)"
      )
    )
  )

shift_share_chart <- ggplot(
  shift_share_long,
  aes(x = contribution_pp, y = waste_stream, fill = effect)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#17212b", linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(
    data = shift_share,
    aes(x = total_contribution_pp, y = waste_stream),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "#17212b",
    stroke = 0.8,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = effect_colours
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(number(x, accuracy = 1), " pp"),
    breaks = c(-6, -4, -2, 0),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.18))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    x = "Contribution to national rate change (percentage points)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = NULL
  ) +
  slide_chart_theme +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.margin = margin(4, 10, 8, 10)
  )

# Interactive priority map

plot_summary <- priority_stream_year |>
  distinct(
    Year,
    median_generated_kt,
    national_recycling_rate

plot_x_max <- ceiling(max(priority_stream_year$generated_kt) / 100) * 100
plot_y_max <- 108

repel_priority_labels <- function(data, x_max, y_max, seed_year) {
  point_positions <- cbind(
    data$generated_plot_kt / x_max,
    data$recycling_rate_plot / y_max
  )

  label_width <- pmin(
    0.235,
    pmax(0.05, nchar(data$chart_label) * 0.0072)
  )
  label_height <- rep(0.036, nrow(data))
  label_centres <- cbind(
    point_positions[, 1],
    pmin(
      0.95,
      pmax(
        0.05,
        point_positions[, 2] +
          if_else(point_positions[, 2] > 0.85, -0.05, 0.05)
      )
    )
  )
  label_boxes <- cbind(
    label_centres[, 1] - label_width / 2,
    label_centres[, 2] - label_height / 2,
    label_centres[, 1] + label_width / 2,
    label_centres[, 2] + label_height / 2
  )

  set.seed(1200 + seed_year)
  repelled <- ggrepel:::repel_boxes2(
    data_points = point_positions,
    point_size = scales::rescale(
      sqrt(pmax(data$disposed_kt, 0)),
      to = c(0.01, 0.05)
    ),
    point_padding_x = 0.006,
    point_padding_y = 0.009,
    boxes = label_boxes,
    xlim = c(0.015, 0.985),
    ylim = c(0.025, 0.975),
    hjust = rep(0.5, nrow(data)),
    vjust = rep(0.5, nrow(data)),
    force_push = 8e-06,
    force_pull = 4e-07,
    max_time = 0.6,
    max_overlaps = Inf,
    max_iter = 12000L,
    direction = "both",
    verbose = 0L
  )

  data |>
    mutate(
      label_generated_plot_kt = repelled$x * x_max,
      label_recycling_rate_plot = repelled$y * y_max,
      label_distance = sqrt(
        ((label_generated_plot_kt - generated_plot_kt) / x_max)^2 +
          ((label_recycling_rate_plot - recycling_rate_plot) / y_max)^2
      )
    )
}

priority_stream_year <- priority_stream_year |>

  group_modify(
    ~ repel_priority_labels(
      .x,
      x_max = plot_x_max,

      seed_year = .y$year
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Render-stopping validation

  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    generated_streams = sum(generated, na.rm = TRUE),
    recycled_streams = sum(recycled, na.rm = TRUE),
    disposed_streams = sum(disposed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    national_year |>
      transmute(
        year,
        generated_published = generated,
        recycled_published = recycled,
        disposed_published = disposed
      ),
    by = "year"
  )

  mutate(balance_gap = abs(generated - recycled - disposed))

  filter(
    year %in% 2014:2024,
    is.na(source_recycling_rate)

# pipeline-step-5-start
pipeline_data_checks <- c(
  source_shape = nrow(raw_waste) == 60 && ncol(raw_waste) == 26 &&
    length(grep("^[0-9]{4}$", names(raw_waste))) == 25,
  tidy_structure = nrow(stream_year) == 14 * 25 &&
    all(c("generated", "recycled", "disposed", "source_recycling_rate") %in%
      names(stream_year)),
  category_coverage = all(!is.na(stream_year$waste_system_category)),
  amount_bounds = all(stream_year$generated >= 0, na.rm = TRUE) &&
    all(stream_year$recycled >= 0, na.rm = TRUE) &&
    all(stream_year$disposed >= 0, na.rm = TRUE) &&
    all(stream_year$generated >= stream_year$recycled, na.rm = TRUE) &&
    all(stream_year$generated >= stream_year$disposed, na.rm = TRUE),
  rate_bounds = all(is.na(stream_year$source_recycling_rate) |
    dplyr::between(stream_year$source_recycling_rate, 0, 100)),
  declared_missingness = nrow(missing_rate_check) == 3 &&
    all(missing_rate_check$waste_stream == "Others") &&
    setequal(missing_rate_check$year, 2022:2024),
  national_reconciliation = max(
    abs(national_check$generated_streams - national_check$generated_published),
    abs(national_check$recycled_streams - national_check$recycled_published),
    abs(national_check$disposed_streams - national_check$disposed_published)
  ) <= 3000,
  stream_arithmetic = max(stream_arithmetic_check$balance_gap,
    na.rm = TRUE) <= 3000,
  published_anchors = isTRUE(all.equal(
    decade_rate_data |> filter(year %in% c(2014, 2024)) |>
      pull(source_recycling_rate),
    c(60, 50)
  ))
)

stopifnot(all(pipeline_data_checks))

presentation_source <- readLines("presentation.qmd", warn = FALSE)

extract_pipeline_code <- function(step) {
  start_marker <- paste0("# pipeline-step-", step, "-start")
  end_marker <- paste0("# pipeline-step-", step, "-end")
  start_line <- match(start_marker, str_trim(presentation_source))
  end_line <- match(end_marker, str_trim(presentation_source))

  stopifnot(
    !is.na(start_line),
    !is.na(end_line),
    end_line > start_line
  )

  paste(
    presentation_source[(start_line + 1):(end_line - 1)],
    collapse = "\n"
  )
}

  1:5,
  function(step) {
    paste(
      highr::hi_html(extract_pipeline_code(step)),
      collapse = "\n"
    )
  }
)

format_pipeline_number <- function(value) {
  format(
    value,
    big.mark = ",",
    scientific = FALSE,
    trim = TRUE
  )
}
```

## Singapore generated 6.66 million tonnes of waste in 2024 {#headline}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
The national system records each tonne in one of two outcomes: recycled or disposed.
:::


::: {.notes}
Good morning/afternoon. We are presenting Two Worlds of Waste: What Singapore's Recycling Rate Hides.

The cover image is Semakau, Singapore's only landfill, which is projected to be full by 2035.

Our project asks whether the national recycling rate tells us enough about where Singapore's waste burden actually comes from.

In 2024, Singapore generated approximately 6.66 million tonnes of waste. Around 3.33 million tonnes were recycled, while another 3.33 million tonnes were disposed of. This gives the published national recycling rate of 50%.

The figure is correct, but it only tells us the overall outcome. It does not show which materials created that result, which streams performed well or poorly, or where most of the disposal burden sits.
:::

## A single 50% rate hides two different questions {#rate-questions-slide}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
It summarises the system, but not where recycling strength and disposal burden originate.
:::

::: {.rate-explainer}

<div class="question-kicker">What the evidence supports</div>

::: {.rate-topic .rate-topic-teal}
<h3><span class="rate-topic-number">01</span>Larger waste streams exert more influence</h3>
<p>A 1,000 kt stream carries ten times the pull of a 100 kt stream because the national rate is weighted by tonnage.</p>
:::

::: {.rate-topic .rate-topic-teal-alt}
<h3><span class="rate-topic-number">02</span>A shrinking high-recycling stream lowers the headline</h3>
<p>When a large industrial stream contracts, its recycled tonnage falls even if its own recycling performance is unchanged.</p>
:::

::: {.rate-question .rate-question-hides .fragment .custom .box-reveal data-fragment-index="1"}

::: {.rate-topic .rate-topic-orange}
<h3><span class="rate-topic-number">03</span>The mix can change, or performance can change</h3>
<p>One percentage cannot distinguish a different waste mix from weaker recycling within individual streams.</p>
:::

::: {.rate-topic .rate-topic-orange-alt}
<h3><span class="rate-topic-number">04</span>The headline cannot locate strength or burden</h3>
<p>It does not show which streams build recycled tonnage or create disposed waste, and those contributions may originate in different places.</p>
:::
:::

```{=html}
<div class="callout callout-question callout-titled rate-transition fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="2" role="note" aria-label="The question this raises">
  <div class="callout-title">The question this raises</div>
  <div class="callout-body">
    <div class="callout-content">
      <p>Does a lower national rate necessarily mean that recycling performance deteriorated across the system?</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

<p class="source-note rate-source">Sources: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA annual dataset</a>; event annotations: <a href="https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/reduction-in-overall-waste-generation-in-2020-with-less-waste-sent-to-semakau-landfill">[1] NEA 2020</a>, <a href="https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/waste-generation-and-recycling-rates-increased-in-2022-as-economic-activity-picked-up">[2] NEA 2022</a>, <a href="https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/singapore-sees-a-decade-of-progress-in-waste-reduction-but-more-can-be-done-for-recycling">[3] NEA 2023</a> and <a href="https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/waste-generation-rate-continues-to-trend-downwards-in-2024">[4] NEA 2024</a>.</p>

::: {.notes}
Singapore's national recycling rate fell from 60% in 2014 to 50% in 2024.

The decade also included major shifts, including the 2020 Circuit Breaker, the recovery in 2022 and fewer demolition projects in the later years.

However, the national rate can fall for two different reasons. First, individual waste streams may be recycling less effectively. This is the performance effect. Second, Singapore may be generating less highly recyclable industrial waste. This changes the waste mix and lowers the national average. This is the mix effect.

These are different problems and require different responses. The national rate alone cannot separate them, which is the main issue our redesign and analysis address.

Handover: Dalton will now explain what the original CNA chart shows, what it leaves hidden and the dataset used for our redesign.
:::

```{=html}
    </div>

<p class="source-note cna-source-note">Sources: <a href="https://www.channelnewsasia.com/singapore/waste-recycling-rates-domestic-statistics-nea-2024-5253106">CNA, 23 July 2025</a>; <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA annual waste-management data via SingStat/Data.gov.sg</a>. Changes calculated from 2014 and 2024 tonnage.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
We started with CNA's July 2025 chart showing Singapore's generated and recycled waste from 2014 to 2024.

Over the decade, total waste generated fell by 11%, from 7.52 million to 6.66 million tonnes. Recycled waste fell faster, by 26%, from 4.47 million to 3.33 million tonnes.

The chart also makes the 2020 dip and the recovery that followed easy to see.

Before critiquing it, the chart has four clear strengths. It is visually simple, uses one consistent unit, makes the national trend easy to understand and uses a familiar chart type that is quick to scan.

However, it also has five important limitations, and each one informed our redesign. First, the recycling rate is not shown directly, so we place it on the y-axis. Second, waste-stream composition is hidden, so each stream becomes a separate bubble positioned by generated tonnage on the x-axis. Third, the chart gives limited actionable insight, so bubble size shows disposed waste directly. Fourth, the generated-waste line receives most of the visual attention, so our redesign balances four dimensions: scale, recycling performance, disposal burden and waste category. Fifth, the chart lacks benchmarks and explanatory detail, so we add the annual national recycling-rate reference, a shaded screening area, hover information and a year slider.

This keeps the original chart's clear decade view, while adding the stream-level detail needed to understand what is driving the result.
:::

::: {.notes}
We used the official MSE and NEA annual waste-management dataset through SingStat and Data.gov.sg. This is the same official source underlying CNA's article.

The full dataset covers 2000 to 2024. Our main analysis uses the same 2014 to 2024 period shown by CNA, which allows a direct comparison between the original visualisation and our redesign.

The dataset includes national totals and 14 published waste streams. One limitation is that the stream labelled Others has no published recycling rate from 2022 to 2024. We retain it in national generated, recycled and disposed totals, but exclude it from analyses that require a stream-level recycling rate. We do not estimate or fill in the missing values.
:::

```{=html}
<p class="preparation-output">Each row represents one waste stream in one year, bringing its generated, recycled and disposed tonnage, recycling rate, category and national context into one record.</p>

```

::: {.notes}
The original CSV is not tidy. It contains four repeated blocks: generated, recycled, disposed and recycling rate.

Each block repeats the same stream names, so the first step is to tag each row by its measurement type. We then standardise the stream names, reshape the years into rows and create one record for each waste stream in each year.

From this cleaned table, we calculate the rate gap, disposal share, recycling contribution and the values used in our later analyses.

Before anything renders, the pipeline runs eight validation checks. These include checking the source structure, expected record count, valid values, arithmetic balance, national reconciliation within three kilotonnes, and the published anchor rates of 60% in 2014 and 50% in 2024. The checks also confirm the declared missing values for Others and the main analytical results.

If any validation check fails, the presentation stops rendering. This means the charts are generated only after the data and results pass the required checks.
:::

<p class="source-note">Source: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA, <em>Waste Management And Overall Recycling Rates, Annual</em></a>, via SingStat/Data.gov.sg.</p>

::: {.notes}
This is our improved interactive visualisation.

Each bubble represents one waste stream. The x-axis shows generated waste. The y-axis shows the recycling rate. Bubble size shows disposed tonnage, while colour shows the waste-system category.

The dashed horizontal line marks the national recycling-rate reference for the selected year. The slider allows the audience to move through the period from 2014 to 2024, with 2024 shown by default. Hovering over a bubble reveals the exact values for that waste stream.

In 2024, ferrous metal and construction and demolition waste sit near the top because they recycle almost all their waste. Their disposal bubbles are therefore relatively small. Plastic, paper and cardboard, and food sit below the national reference with large generated volumes and large disposal bubbles.

The shaded area identifies streams with above-median generated volume and below-reference recycling. This is a descriptive screening rule, not an official policy target.

A low recycling rate alone does not automatically make a stream a national priority, especially if the stream is very small. Similarly, a large stream is not necessarily a major problem if most of it is already recycled.

By combining volume, recycling performance and disposal burden, the chart gives a more complete picture. Both the screening rule and the direct disposal ranking identify the same three priority streams: plastic, paper and cardboard, and food.
:::

```{=html}
      <h3>Plastic leads the disposal burden</h3>
      <p>Plastic is <strong>26.3%</strong> of disposal and only <strong>1.3%</strong> of recycling; paper/cardboard and food also carry substantial burdens.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="mismatch-takeaway fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="2">
      <span class="mismatch-takeaway-title">Key takeaway</span>
      <p>Most major streams sit far from the equal-shares line. The streams strengthening the recycling total are not those creating most of the disposal burden.</p>
    </div>
```
:::
:::

<p class="mismatch-method-note">All 14 published waste streams are included. Distance from the equality line shows the continuous contribution gap; colour reinforces its direction and magnitude. Light deterministic jitter separates edge points, while ggrepel positions labels. No classification threshold is applied.</p>

```{=html}
<p class="source-note">Source: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA, <em>Waste Management And Overall Recycling Rates, Annual</em></a>, via SingStat/Data.gov.sg, 2024.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
P1 compares each stream's share of national recycling with its share of national disposal in 2024.

The dashed diagonal represents equal contribution. A point above the line contributes more to recycling than disposal, while a point below the line contributes more to disposal than recycling.

Ferrous metal is strongly recycling-heavy. It contributes 38.1% of recycled waste, but only 0.2% of disposed waste.

Plastic shows almost the opposite pattern. It contributes 26.3% of disposal, but only 1.3% of recycling.

Together, plastic, paper and cardboard, and food account for 71.8% of all disposed waste in 2024.

This shows that the streams strengthening Singapore's recycling total are not the same streams creating most of the disposal burden. That is the main idea behind our title, Two Worlds of Waste.
:::

<p class="rate-gap-method-note">Cell labels show signed percentage-point gaps. Published integer rates are shown for the 13 streams with complete 2014–2024 observations. Grey 2018 cells fall below the displayed −55 pp scale and are not missing. “Others” is excluded because no rate is published for 2022–2024. <p class="source-note">Source: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA, <em>Waste Management And Overall Recycling Rates, Annual</em></a>, via SingStat/Data.gov.sg, 2014–2024.</p>

::: {.notes}
P2 asks whether weak recycling in the priority streams is temporary or persistent.

This heatmap shows each stream's recycling-rate gap from the annual national reference for the 13 streams with complete published rates from 2014 to 2024.

Plastic, paper and cardboard, and food remain below the national reference in all eleven years. This shows that their weaker recycling performance is persistent rather than a one-year fluctuation.

However, low recycling alone does not define priority. In the 2024 cross-section, generated volume and recycling rate show almost no rank association, with a Spearman's rho of 0.017. This means larger waste streams do not automatically recycle better or worse.

The heatmap shows persistence, while the priority map adds generated volume and disposal burden. Together, they identify the streams where weak recycling occurs at a nationally important scale.
:::

::: {.slide-subtitle}


::: {.notes}
Before we break down why the national recycling rate fell, it helps to first look at what happened to recycled tonnage.

From 2014 to 2024, around 81% of the decline in recycled tonnage came from just three highly recycled industrial streams. Construction and demolition waste fell by 554 kilotonnes, used slag fell by 251 kilotonnes, and ferrous metal fell by 121 kilotonnes.

These materials already have very high recycling rates. So when less of them was generated, there was naturally less of them available to be recycled.

However, the everyday-material streams did not all follow the same pattern. Food recycling actually increased by 37 kilotonnes, while paper and cardboard recycling fell by 244 kilotonnes.

This gives us an important clue. The fall in recycled tonnage was not caused by every waste stream performing worse. Part of it came from Singapore simply generating less of the industrial waste that is usually recycled at very high rates.

But tonnage alone still cannot tell us how much of the decline came from a change in the waste mix, and how much came from weaker recycling performance.

Also, the 81% here refers only to the decline in recycled tonnage. The next slide looks at the decline in the national recycling rate itself.
:::

## P3: Shift-share decomposition (2) {#decomposition-slide}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
Shift-share separates changes in what Singapore generated from changes in how well each stream was recycled; white circles mark net stream effects.
:::

```{r}
shift_share_chart
```
:::
<p class="decomposition-method-note">Symmetric shift-share allocates the interaction equally. The components total −9.5 pp; the remaining 0.5 pp to the published ten-point change reflects source rounding. A separate counterfactual robustness check is provided in the appendix.</p>
```{=html}

  <div class="callout-title">Key takeaway</div>
  <div class="callout-body">
    <div class="callout-content">
      <p>Composition explains <strong>68%</strong> of the reconstructed rate decline; this is distinct from the prior 81% result about lost recycled tonnage.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.chart-commentary .decomposition-commentary}
```{=html}
    <div class="decomposition-result decomposition-mix fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="0">
      <span class="question-kicker">Mix effect</span>
      <div class="decomposition-result-line">
        <strong>−6.5 pp</strong>
        <span>68% of reconstructed decline</span>
      </div>
      <p>Changes in the relative volumes of waste streams produced most of the fall.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="decomposition-result decomposition-rate fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="1">
      <span class="question-kicker">Performance effect</span>
      <div class="decomposition-result-line">
        <strong>−3.0 pp</strong>
        <span>32% of reconstructed decline</span>
      </div>
      <p>Changes in recycling performance within streams still reduced the national result.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="decomposition-contributors fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="2">
      <span class="question-kicker">Main contributors</span>
      <h3>Industrial streams drove composition; paper/cardboard drove performance.</h3>
      <p>Construction and demolition and used slag dominate the mix effect. Paper/cardboard contributes the largest negative performance effect.</p>
    </div>
```
:::
:::

```{=html}
<p class="source-note decomposition-source">Source: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA, <em>Waste Management And Overall Recycling Rates, Annual</em></a>, via SingStat/Data.gov.sg, 2014 and 2024.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
To separate these two reasons, we use a method called shift-share decomposition. In simple terms, it breaks the decline into two parts.

The first is the mix effect. This looks at how the national rate changed because Singapore generated different proportions of each waste stream. The second is the performance effect. This looks at how the national rate changed because individual streams recycled better or worse.

Our results show a negative 6.5 percentage-point mix effect and a negative 3.0 percentage-point performance effect. This means around 68% of the reconstructed decline came from the changing waste mix, while the remaining 32% came from actual changes in recycling performance.

Construction and demolition waste and used slag were the main drivers of the mix effect because their share of total waste became smaller. For the performance effect, paper and cardboard had the largest negative contribution. Its recycling rate fell from 52% in 2014 to 32% in 2024.

The two effects add up to around negative 9.5 percentage points, instead of the full published ten-point drop. This small difference is because the source values are rounded.

So the main takeaway is that Singapore's falling recycling rate does not mean every waste stream suddenly became much worse at recycling. Most of the decline came from generating less highly recyclable industrial waste, although there was still a real performance decline in some streams, especially paper and cardboard.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="conclusion-thesis">
  <p>The decline was largely compositional, while the 2024 disposal burden was concentrated in three waste streams.</p>
</div>

<div class="conclusion-column-grid">
  <div class="conclusion-column fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="0">
    <div class="conclusion-metric conclusion-metric-headline">
      <span class="conclusion-kicker">Headline</span>

    </div>
    <div class="conclusion-context">

      <p><strong>Singapore generated and recycled less waste in 2024 than in 2014.</strong> The major turning points reflect the 2020 Circuit Breaker, the 2022 recovery, fewer demolition projects and lower steel-smelting activity.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

      <span class="conclusion-kicker">Cause</span>

      <h4>of the reconstructed decline came from a changed waste mix</h4>
      <p>Explains why the rate fell.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="conclusion-context conclusion-performance-context">
      <span class="conclusion-kicker">Performance context</span>
      <p>Stream-level performance explains the remaining <strong>32%</strong> of the reconstructed decline. Paper/cardboard made the largest negative performance contribution.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

      <p>Shows where the burden sits.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="conclusion-context">
      <span class="conclusion-kicker">Two material worlds</span>
      <p><strong>Construction, slag and metals</strong> dominate recycled tonnage. Plastic, paper/cardboard and food combine large volumes with persistently low recycling rates and dominate disposal.</p>

<p class="conclusion-takeaway fragment custom box-reveal" data-fragment-index="3">The national rate tells us what happened. Generated tonnes, recycling rates and disposed tonnes reveal where the burden sits.</p>

<p class="source-note conclusion-source">Sources: <a href="https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_daf568968ab40dc81e7b08887a83c8fa/view">MSE and NEA annual waste-management data via SingStat/Data.gov.sg</a>, 2014 and 2024; NEA media releases on the 2020–2024 turning points.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
To conclude, there are three main numbers to remember.

First, 50% is Singapore's national recycling rate in 2024.

Second, 68% explains why the reconstructed rate declined. Most of the fall came from a change in the waste mix, rather than every stream suddenly recycling worse.

Third, 71.8% shows where the current disposal burden is concentrated: in plastic, paper and cardboard, and food.

Together, these findings reveal what we mean by two worlds of waste. Construction waste, slag and metals contribute most of the recycled tonnage, while plastic, paper and cardboard, and food contribute most of the disposed waste.

So, the national recycling rate tells us what happened, but the stream-level generated, recycled and disposed tonnes help explain why it happened and where attention is most needed.

At the same time, our analysis only identifies the priority streams. It does not prove the behavioural, collection, market or policy reasons behind their outcomes. Those causes would require further investigation.

Thank you. We are happy to take questions.
:::

## Q&A {#qa-slide .plain-closing}

::: {.notes}
Prepared answers:

- Two decomposition methods differ because the sequential counterfactual is order-dependent, while the symmetric method allocates the interaction evenly. Both reconstruct minus 9.5 points.
- “Others” is not imputed because the source publishes no rate from 2022. It stays in reconciliation and does not change the priority ranking.
- Disposed waste is encoded directly because it is the operational burden and because inferring it would repeat the original chart’s weakness.
- The median volume threshold is transparent, distribution-free and recomputed per year, but the high-volume, low-recycling area is not an official benchmark.
- Composition is not a circular explanation. The counterfactual quantifies it: applying 2024 rates to the 2014 mix still gives 56.9%, so a genuine 2.6-point sequential performance loss remains.
- The 2020 disruption does not determine the decomposition because the comparison uses the 2014 and 2024 endpoints. It remains visible in the interactive decade view.
- A single bubble chart was preferred to small multiples because the argument requires generated scale, recycling performance and disposal burden to be read together.
- The analysis is descriptive. Annual national totals cannot identify contamination, collection channel or policy causality.
- The 81% and 68% figures use different denominators. The first explains lost recycled tonnes; the second decomposes the recycling-rate change.
- A lower national rate is not automatically a worse overall outcome. Total generation fell 11%, while the changing mix of highly recycled industrial streams pulled the rate down.
- The priority set is robust to the high-volume, low-recycling boundary: a direct ranking by disposed tonnage identifies the same three streams.
:::

## Appendix: Six questions we would answer differently now {#appendix-reflection-slide .plain-closing data-visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
Looking back, these were the moments that changed how we understood the project.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="reflection-grid">
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-teal">
    <h3><span>01:</span> Why did we look beyond the headline?</h3>
    <h4>Timothy Chia</h4>
    <p>When I first saw CNA’s chart, the story seemed straightforward: Singapore generated less waste, but the recycling rate also fell from 60% in 2014 to 50% in 2024. I initially thought our job was just to make that decline easier to see.</p>
    <p>Once we started asking why it happened, however, I realised the national totals could not tell us which materials created the disposal burden, which streams contributed most to recycled tonnage, or whether every stream had actually become worse. That changed the direction of our work. We kept the headline because it gives useful context, but treated it as the question we needed to investigate rather than the answer we had to repeat.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-orange">
    <h3><span>02:</span> What actually took the most work?</h3>
    <h4>Dalton Chng</h4>
    <p>I expected most of our time to go into plotting, but the hardest part came before the first chart. The source looked like a normal 60 × 26 table, yet generated, recycled, disposed and recycling-rate values were stored in four repeated blocks. A row could not be interpreted safely until we identified which metric block it belonged to. We tagged those blocks, reshaped them into 350 stream-year records and checked that the totals still matched the published figures.</p>
    <p>Only then could we derive disposal, rate gaps, contribution shares and stream groups from one consistent structure. It was less visible than the final charts, but this work stopped us from copying values by hand and made every later revision much safer.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-teal">
    <h3><span>03:</span> How did the proposal help us?</h3>
    <h4>Pham Anh Bao Khang</h4>
    <p>For me, the proposal was most useful because it forced us to state what we wanted to test before we became attached to a particular chart. It gave us the three analysis questions, the stream-year structure, the priority-map idea and an early validation plan.</p>
    <p>Still, our final work did not follow it word for word. While analysing the data, we added the rate-gap heatmap, rank check, shift-share decomposition and counterfactual because each one answered a new doubt that the proposal had not fully resolved. We also learnt that an interactive chart should add exploration, not carry the whole argument. The proposal therefore became a plan we could question and improve, rather than a conclusion that our results were expected to defend.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-orange">
    <h3><span>04:</span> What result surprised us most?</h3>
    <h4>Sitt Min Naing</h4>
    <p>I was surprised that a lower national recycling rate did not mean every waste stream had become worse. Plastic, paper/cardboard and food were still the clearest 2024 priorities because they combined high generated volume with weak recycling and together formed most of the disposal burden.</p>
    <p>However, the decade decline had another explanation: highly recycled industrial streams made up a smaller share of total waste in 2024. In our symmetric decomposition, this changing mix accounted for 6.5 points of the reconstructed 9.5-point fall. Recycling performance still mattered, especially for paper/cardboard, but it was not the whole story. This result made us separate two claims that we had originally treated as one: where action is needed now, and why the national rate changed.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-teal">
    <h3><span>05:</span> What did we have to correct?</h3>
    <h4>Ang Ben Rong</h4>
    <p>One useful part of the project was realising that some proposal wording went beyond what the dataset could support. We had contrasted industrial recycling with “consumer-facing” waste because it sounded intuitive. The source, however, identifies material streams, not whether waste came from households, businesses or industrial activity.</p>
    <p>We changed the label to “everyday materials”, made all four groups explicitly analyst-defined and explained that they were for navigation rather than official NEA classifications. We also avoided claiming that behaviour, contamination, collection or processing capacity caused the patterns because those variables were unavailable. The wording became less dramatic, but it made our interpretation more responsible and easier to defend.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="reflection-item reflection-orange">
    <h3><span>06:</span> What would we improve next?</h3>
    <h4>Timothy · Dalton · Khang · Sitt · Ben</h4>
    <p>As a team, we would keep validation inside the analysis rather than treating it as a final checklist. Our deck now stops if the source shape changes, the arithmetic fails, national totals no longer reconcile or a headline result moves unexpectedly. We also left the unpublished “Others” rates missing instead of filling them, because a complete-looking series was not worth inventing unsupported values.</p>
    <p>If we continued the project, we would user-test whether people understand the bubble size, national reference line, highlighted priority area and year control without explanation. We would also look for origin-sector, contamination, collection and processing data. Those additions would help us move beyond describing what changed and towards explaining why it changed and which interventions might realistically work.</p>
  </article>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The original CNA visualisation was useful and accurate for the national trend, but it answered a narrower question. Our redesign moved from aggregate description to stream-level diagnosis by restructuring the same official NEA and MSE source.

The proposal remained active throughout the project. It established the weaknesses to address, the stream-year data model, three analytical questions, the interactive priority map and the validation plan. The final build retained those foundations while adding the persistent rate-gap heatmap, Spearman rank check, stream-level change analysis, symmetric shift-share decomposition and counterfactual test.

The data-engineering work converted a 60-row by 26-column source with four repeated metric blocks into 350 stream-year observations covering 14 streams and 25 years. Derived fields included generated, recycled and disposed kilotonnes, recycling-rate gaps, contribution shares and analyst-defined categories. Automated checks covered dimensions, metric blocks, record counts, ranges, arithmetic, national reconciliation, published references, expected missingness and headline conclusions.

The most important responsible decision was not estimating the unpublished recycling rates for "Others" from 2022 to 2024. "Others" remains in national tonnage reconciliation and is excluded only where a published stream rate is required.

The priority map was chosen because generated volume, recycling rate and disposed tonnage answer different questions. Reading them together identifies action priorities more responsibly than ranking by only one measure. The supporting analyses showed that plastic, paper/cardboard and food remain central to the disposal burden, while the national recycling-rate decline mainly reflects the smaller share of highly recycled industrial streams. Performance still mattered, particularly for paper/cardboard.

We corrected the proposal's earlier industrial-versus-consumer framing because the source records material streams, not household, commercial or industrial origin. The final presentation therefore uses analyst-defined groupings and does not claim causes involving behaviour, contamination, collection, processing capacity or commodity markets.

With more time, we would test whether viewers understand bubble size, the national reference, the highlighted action region and the year control. We would also seek origin-sector and operational datasets to move from descriptive diagnosis towards stronger causal explanation and policy recommendations.
:::

## Appendix: Methods and limitations {#appendix-methods-slide .plain-closing data-visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
The principal assumptions are visible so the analysis can be challenged and reproduced.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="appendix-method-grid">
  <div class="appendix-method">
    <span class="question-kicker">National arithmetic</span>
    <h3>Published rates are retained</h3>
    <p>Exact tonnage-derived rates are used for decomposition; published integer rates are used for headline references. This explains the reconstructed 59.5% versus published 60% in 2014.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="appendix-method">
    <span class="question-kicker">Missing values</span>
    <h3>No recycling rates are imputed</h3>
    <p>“Others” is retained when reconciling national tonnage but excluded from rate-based 2022–2024 plotting where the source publishes no rate.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="appendix-method">
    <span class="question-kicker">Decomposition</span>
    <h3>Primary result is symmetric</h3>
    <p>The shift-share method averages endpoint weights and rates, allocating the mix-rate interaction equally. The fixed-2014-mix scenario is a separate sequential robustness check.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="appendix-method">
    <span class="question-kicker">Interpretation</span>
    <h3>Descriptive, not causal</h3>
    <p>The analysis identifies accounting contributions and priority streams. The median and national-rate boundaries are recalculated each year; the shaded area is not an NEA target or definitive policy ranking, and the analysis does not estimate causal effects.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Appendix: Symmetric shift-share equations {#appendix-shift-share-equations-slide .plain-closing data-visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
Midpoint weights separate composition and performance while reconstructing the tonnage-derived endpoint change exactly.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="shift-equation-layout">
  <div class="shift-equation-rate">
    <span class="question-kicker">Tonnage-reconstructed national rate</span>
    <div class="shift-equation-math">\(R_t^{*} = \sum_i w_{i,t}r_{i,t}\)</div>
    <div class="shift-equation-definitions">
      <p><strong>\(w_{i,t}\)</strong> is stream \(i\)'s share of generated waste in year \(t\).</p>
      <p><strong>\(r_{i,t}\)</strong> is its exact recycling rate, calculated from recycled and generated tonnage.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="shift-equation-grid">
    <div class="shift-equation-panel shift-equation-mix">
      <span class="question-kicker">Mix effect</span>
      <div class="shift-equation-math">\(M_i = (w_{i,2024}-w_{i,2014})\left(\frac{r_{i,2014}+r_{i,2024}}{2}\right)\times100\)</div>
      <p>Changes in each stream's share of total generated waste, evaluated at its average recycling rate.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="shift-equation-panel shift-equation-performance">
      <span class="question-kicker">Performance effect</span>
      <div class="shift-equation-math">\(P_i = (r_{i,2024}-r_{i,2014})\left(\frac{w_{i,2014}+w_{i,2024}}{2}\right)\times100\)</div>
      <p>Changes in each stream's recycling rate, evaluated at its average share of generated waste.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="shift-equation-reconstruction">
    <div>
      <span class="question-kicker">Exact reconstruction</span>
      <div class="shift-equation-math">\(\sum_i(M_i+P_i)=R_{2024}^{*}-R_{2014}^{*}=50.0\%-59.5\%=-9.5\text{ pp}\)</div>
    </div>
    <p><strong>Why midpoint weights?</strong> Averaging both endpoints divides the mix-performance interaction equally, so the split is symmetric and independent of which year is treated first. Multiplication by 100 expresses each contribution in percentage points.</p>
  </div>

  <p class="shift-equation-note"><strong>Rounding:</strong> the published headline moves from 60% to 50%. The decomposition uses exact tonnage and therefore starts at 59.5%. The appendix counterfactual is a sequential robustness check, so its component split is order-dependent and is not expected to match the symmetric split.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Use this slide only if the audience asks how the 68% and 32% contributions were calculated. Emphasise that the two equations reconstruct the exact tonnage-derived change and that midpoint averaging prevents the answer from depending on which endpoint is applied first.

The published national rate is rounded to a whole percentage. The 2014 reconstructed rate is 59.5%, which rounds to the published 60%; the 2024 reconstructed rate is 50.0%.
:::

## Appendix: Counterfactual robustness check {#appendix-counterfactual-slide data-visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.slide-subtitle}
Holding composition at 2014 levels tests whether 2024 stream rates alone can reproduce the 50% headline.
:::

::: {.chart-commentary-layout .counterfactual-layout}
::: {.chart-frame .chart-frame-counterfactual .chart-r-output}
```{r}
#| label: presentation-counterfactual-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-retina: 2
#| fig-format: svg
#| out-width: 100%
counterfactual_chart
```
:::

::: {.chart-commentary .counterfactual-commentary}
```{=html}
    <div class="counterfactual-values">
      <div><span>2014 reconstructed</span><strong>59.5%</strong></div>
      <div><span>2024 rates on 2014 mix</span><strong>56.9%</strong></div>
      <div><span>2024 reconstructed</span><strong>50.0%</strong></div>
    </div>
    <div class="robustness-verdict">
      <span class="question-kicker">Robustness result</span>
      <strong>Only 2.6 percentage points disappear when stream rates change but the 2014 mix is held fixed.</strong>
      <p>The larger gap appears only when the 2024 waste mix is introduced.</p>
    </div>
    <p class="counterfactual-takeaway">A second method supports the same conclusion: the national decline is mostly compositional, not a uniform collapse in recycling performance.</p>
    <p class="method-note"><strong>Method note:</strong> this sequential scenario is order-dependent. The main −6.5/−3.0 pp result uses a symmetric allocation, so the two splits should not be numerically identical. Neither method establishes causality.</p>
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Use this appendix slide only if the audience asks for a robustness check. Applying 2024 stream rates to the 2014 mix produces 56.9%, well above the actual 50%.

The sequential and symmetric splits differ because the sequential result depends on which change is applied first. Both reconstruct the same endpoint change and support the same qualitative conclusion. Neither identifies causality.
:::
